title: Used To / Be Used To / When vs. While
subtitle: Talk about finished past habits, being accustomed to something, and connect two past events precisely.
objectives: Use "used to" for finished past habits
Use "be used to" for being accustomed/familiar with something

content.intro: "Used to" and "be used to" look almost identical but mean completely different things — this lesson also reviews when to use "when" versus "while" in past narratives.

rules.heading: a) Used to — a finished past habit
rules.body:
Subject + used to + infinitive. Describes something true repeatedly in the past, not true now.

  • Affirmative: I used to live in a small village.
  • Negative: She didn't use to like vegetables.
  • Question: Did you use to play the piano?

rules.heading: b) Be used to — accustomed/familiar with
rules.body:
Subject + am/is/are (+not) + used to + noun/-ing. Describes something normal/familiar for someone — not a past habit at all.

  • Affirmative: He is used to driving on the left.
  • Negative: They aren't used to the hot weather here.
  • Question: Are you used to eating spicy food?

rules.heading: c) When vs. while
rules.body:
• When + past simple = a shorter or interrupting action.
  • While + -ing = a longer, background action happening at the same time as another.

examples: I used to live in a small village. Now I live in a big city.
He is used to driving on the left — it's normal for him.
Did you use to play the piano as a child?
Are you used to eating spicy food?
When I arrived home, it started to rain.
I was cooking while my wife was watching TV.

commonMistakes.wrong: I used to living in a small village.
commonMistakes.right: I used to live in a small village.
commonMistakes.why: "Used to" is followed by the infinitive (live), not the -ing form.

commonMistakes.wrong: He is used to drive on the left.
commonMistakes.right: He is used to driving on the left.
commonMistakes.why: "Be used to" is followed by a noun or the -ing form, not the infinitive.

commonMistakes.wrong: I use to play soccer when I was young.
commonMistakes.right: I used to play soccer when I was young.
commonMistakes.why: The affirmative form is "used to," not "use to" — "use to" only appears after "did/didn't."

commonMistakes.wrong: While I arrived home, it started to rain.
commonMistakes.right: When I arrived home, it started to rain.
commonMistakes.why: A short, sudden action (arriving) needs "when," not "while."

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct form: used to, didn't use to, is/are used to, or isn't/aren't used to.

items.prompt: When I was young, I ___ (play) outside every day.
items.explanation: A finished past habit — "used to" + infinitive.

items.prompt: Maria ___ (not/live) alone, so she sometimes feels lonely now.
items.explanation: Negative past habit — "didn't use to" + infinitive.

items.prompt: He ___ (the cold winter) because he comes from a warm country. (not accustomed)
items.explanation: Not accustomed to something — "isn't used to" + noun.
Question form of a past habit: Did + subject + use to + infinitive.

items.prompt: ___ I arrived home, it started to rain.
I was cooking ___ my wife was watching TV.
items.explanation: Two longer background actions happening together — "while."

items.incorrect: He is used to drive on the left.
answer: He is used to driving on the left.
items.explanation: "Be used to" needs the -ing form, not the infinitive.

items.incorrect: I use to play the piano as a child.
answer: I used to play the piano as a child.
items.explanation: The affirmative form is "used to," not "use to."

summary: Used to + infinitive = a finished past habit, not true now.
Be used to + noun/-ing = accustomed/familiar with something, in any tense.
When + past simple = short/interrupting; while + -ing = longer/background.
